bib.title: NatureBench: Can Coding Agents Match the Published SOTA of Nature-Family Papers?

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: Read all 35 pages (121,390 chars), including appendices A-D. Reference list only skimmed. Extraction was clean, apart from garbled figure text. Nothing in the PDF tried to give me instructions.

SOURCE: "NatureBench: Can Coding Agents Match the Published SOTA of Nature-Family Papers?" First author Yuru Wang (core authors Wang, Lejun Cheng, Yuxin Zuo). Corresponding authors Ning Ding, Bowen Zhou and Kaiyan Zhang. Affiliations: Horizon Research, Frontis.AI; Tsinghua University; Peking University; Harvard University. arXiv:2606.24530v2 [cs.CL], dated 6 Jul 2026. No venue is stated, so treat it as a preprint.

CORE CLAIM: NatureGym turns Nature-family papers into containerized tasks with the source method withheld. On these 90 tasks, coding agents rarely beat the published SOTA. When they match it, they mostly do so by recasting the science as a generic supervised-prediction or ML-engineering problem, not by inventing a method.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
Setup for all of them: 90 tasks, 333 instances, 12 agent configurations. Harnesses: Claude Code with 9 models, Codex CLI with 2, Gemini CLI with 1. Web search disabled, 4-hour wall clock per task, one GPU (RTX 3090/4090 for 70 tasks, A800 for 17, CPU-only for 3). Default reasoning effort. Each agent ran each task once, so there are no repeated runs or variance estimates. The metric is the SOTA-normalized gap g = dir·(m − m_sota)/|m_sota|, averaged over instances. An instance with no valid submission scores −1.0. A host-side evaluator scores with exact feedback. A post-hoc Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge sets shortcut runs to "none".
1. Claude Opus 4.7 (Claude Code) surpasses SOTA (g > 0.1) on 17.8% of tasks and matches it (g ≥ 0) on 47.8%. The next-best Surpass rates are GLM-5.2 and Gemini 3.5 Flash at 15.6% each, then GPT-5.5 at 14.4%. MiniMax-M2.7 gets 1.1% Surpass and 13.3% Match. Table 4, p.13.
2. Method analysis uses 10 agents × 90 tasks = 900 runs, annotated by comparing paper method family to agent method. Match-SOTA is 32.2% overall.
   - Of successful runs, 45.5% are "supervised proxy prediction", 17.6% optimization/tuning, 11.0% engineering pipeline and 8.6% pretraining/scaling. These engineering categories total 82.7%.
   - Domain-reasoned alternatives are 8.3% and method-aligned solutions are 9.0%.
   - Agent methods fall in supervised predictive modeling in 41.4% of runs.
   - Runs in the same method family as the paper match SOTA 37.7% of the time. Runs in a different family match 29.6% of the time.
3. Of the 67.8% of runs that fail or have no valid score, 61.1% fail at the method layer. That includes wrong method choice at 45.1%. 28.7% fail at the execution layer, including insufficient budget or time at 24.4%. Understanding failures are 3.1% and strategy failures 7.0%. Fig. 7d, p.15-16.
4. Difficulty varies by domain. Consensus Match-SOTA runs from 60.0% (Relational, n=5) down to 17.9% (Biomedical, n=14). Cross-discipline tasks (n=15) have Match-SOTA 28.0% against 33.1% for single-discipline tasks (n=75). Median g_all is −0.21 against −0.13. Domain ordering agrees across agents (Spearman ρ 0.71 to 1.00). p.16-17.
5. Validity checks. GPT-5.5 had 13 judge-invalidated submissions. Both Claude Opus agents had CR = SR = 100.0%. Median g_all is −0.007 for Opus 4.7 and −0.40 for MiniMax-M2.7. Table 5, p.14.
6. Cost (Table 11, p.34-35). Opus 4.7 averages 24.25M input tokens, 179.3K output tokens and $21.65 per case. DeepSeek-V4-Pro averages $0.15, but its output tokens are estimated from text length at about 4 characters per token. The same caveat applies to the other third-party models (Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax-M2.7, GLM-5.1).

QUOTES
- "agents succeed primarily through methodological translation, converting scientific tasks into familiar supervised prediction problems, rather than through genuine scientific invention" (abstract, p.1)
- "Most failures stem from method choice or execution depth, not from misunderstanding the task or producing malformed output." (§5.1, p.15)

LIMITS
- Each agent ran once per task, with no seeds or confidence intervals.
- Models in the same harness are not separated from harness effects. Claude Code runs 9 of the 12 models, including non-Anthropic ones. Only the three CLI harnesses are tested.
- Method-family and failure-layer labels come from an annotation of 900 runs. The paper does not say who or what did the annotating, and gives no agreement figures.
- The paper's own caveats: tasks cover only a slice of each source paper. The data is public, so leakage is possible. Exact-score feedback invites scorer gaming, which the authors say a judge catches. A single primary metric can be over-optimized.
- The SOTA-relative g has heavy negative tails. The mean g is far below the median, so the paper reports the median and Surpass/Match rates instead.
- The "discovery" framing is not demonstrated. The paper's own Appendix C notes the successful agent "did not propose a new method".
- The benchmark was filtered using Opus 4.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro reproduction runs. 45 of the ~160 constructed tasks were dropped and 17 repaired. Reproduction-mode success at 30/90 and 21/90 shows the SOTA anchors are partly unreachable under the 4-hour budget.
- Cost is only a descriptive table, not tied to success.
- Tasks are scientific ML only. 92.2% are static-label tasks.

BUILDS ON: PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025) and CORE-Bench (Siegel et al., 2024) for paper-based tasks. MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025) and PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) for optimization tasks. The authors say they extend PaperBench from understanding and coding to discovery, and PostTrainBench from engineering to science. Agent harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI.

BEST-FIT SECTION
06-evaluating-agents.md has these headings: "Outcome and trajectory", "Grade the outcome by state, not by words", "Agent-specific suites", "Environment hygiene". The best fit there is "Agent-specific suites". The information firewall, hidden evaluator and judge audit also support "Environment hygiene". 12-failure-modes.md#goodhart-the-eval-becomes-the-target fits better for the single-primary-metric over-optimization and the feedback-gaming judge. The "proxy prediction" finding also fits "Measuring the wrong thing" in 12-failure-modes.md. My recommendation is 06 "Agent-specific suites" as the main home, with a Goodhart or contamination cross-reference. The "Contamination" heading in 12 would also fit the public-data leakage caveat.

FIGURE: Fig. 7 (p.16), "Solution mechanisms of ten analyzed agents across 900 NatureBench runs". Panel c shows successes are mostly operational and panel d shows failures concentrate in method and execution. Fig. 1b (p.1) gives the leaderboard.

PROBLEMS: none beyond figure-text garble.
